code.title: Primary, unique and foreign keys enforced by the database
code.python:
import sqlite3

# In-memory database; SQLite needs this pragma to enforce foreign keys
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Customers (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Email TEXT UNIQUE)")  # PK + unique key
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, CustomerId INTEGER NOT NULL "
           "REFERENCES Customers(Id))")                                          # foreign key
db.execute("INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1, 'ann@example.com')")

def attempt(label, sql):
    try:
        db.execute(sql)
        print(label, "-> ok")
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
        print(label, "-> rejected:", e)

attempt("duplicate primary key   ", "INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1, 'bob@example.com')")
attempt("duplicate unique email  ", "INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (2, 'ann@example.com')")
attempt("order for missing parent", "INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (10, 99)")
attempt("order for customer 1    ", "INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (10, 1)")
# Cost: each check uses an index lookup, O(log n) per insert; space O(n) for the indexes.

followUps:
A composite key is a key made of two or more columns that are unique only as a pair. Use it when no single column identifies a row, most often in a link table.

Example: OrderLines(OrderId, LineNo). Order 7 can have line 1, and order 8 can also have line 1, but (7,1) appears once. Many-to-many tables such as StudentCourses(StudentId, CourseId) use the same idea, and the pair stops enrolling someone twice. The cost is that every child table pointing at it must carry all the columns, so some teams prefer a single surrogate id instead.

I prefer a surrogate key (an int identity or a sequential GUID) as the primary key, and I keep a unique constraint on the natural key.

Natural keys such as an email, a tax number or a product code look attractive, but they change (people change email), they can be reused, and they are wide, which makes every foreign key and index bigger. A surrogate never changes and is small. The unique constraint on the natural value still stops duplicate business data. Exception: stable, tiny code tables such as country codes ('GB') are fine as natural keys.

NO ACTION (the default) refuses to delete a parent row that still has children. CASCADE silently deletes the children together with the parent.

Example: deleting customer 5 who has 3 orders. With NO ACTION the statement fails with a foreign key error. With CASCADE the 3 orders go too. Cascade is handy for true parts of an aggregate (order lines of an order) but dangerous between independent entities, because one stray delete can wipe a lot of data and take locks on many rows. Other options are SET NULL and SET DEFAULT.

BCNF is a stricter 3NF: every column that determines other columns must itself be a candidate key. 3NF still allows one odd case that BCNF removes.

Example: a table (Student, Course, Teacher) where each teacher teaches only one course. Teacher determines Course, but Teacher is not a key, so the table breaks BCNF even though it can satisfy 3NF. Fix: split into (Teacher, Course) and (Student, Teacher). In practice, if you reach 3NF you are nearly always at BCNF as well.

An update anomaly means one fact is stored in many rows, so changing it in only some of them leaves the data contradicting itself.

Example: an Orders table that repeats CustomerCity on every order. A customer with 40 orders moves from Leeds to York; an update that fixes 38 rows leaves 2 rows saying Leeds, and reports now disagree. The cure is to store the city once in Customers and join to it. The same table also shows insert anomalies (cannot save a customer without an order) and delete anomalies.

Not necessarily. 1NF says each column holds one atomic value per row, but a JSON column is fine when you treat it as one opaque value that you store and return whole.

It becomes a design smell when you query inside it often, filter or join on its parts, or keep a list of repeating items (such as phone numbers) that really belong in a child table. SQL Server has JSON_VALUE and a native json type in newer versions, and you can index a computed column over a JSON property. Use JSON for flexible, rarely queried extras, and normal columns for core data.

Yes, in SQL Server: TRUNCATE is minimally logged yet it is still transactional, so inside a transaction you can roll it back.

Example: BEGIN TRAN; TRUNCATE TABLE Staging; ROLLBACK; brings all rows back. After a committed TRUNCATE there is no undo except a restore. Note that Oracle and MySQL commit implicitly on TRUNCATE, so the answer differs between products. TRUNCATE also resets identity, needs ALTER permission and fails if a foreign key references the table.

A correlated subquery is a subquery that uses a column from the outer query, so conceptually it runs once for each outer row.

Example: SELECT Name FROM Employees e WHERE Salary > (SELECT AVG(Salary) FROM Employees WHERE DeptId = e.DeptId) finds people paid above their own department average. The optimizer often rewrites it as a join, but a window function (AVG(Salary) OVER (PARTITION BY DeptId)) is usually clearer and cheaper. EXISTS subqueries are the common correlated form.

COUNT(*) counts every row; COUNT(column) counts only the rows where that column is not NULL.

Example: a table of 10 customers where 3 have no phone number gives COUNT(*) = 10 and COUNT(Phone) = 7. COUNT(DISTINCT Phone) counts unique non-null values. COUNT(1) behaves the same as COUNT(*). This is a frequent source of wrong totals after a left join, where unmatched rows have NULLs.

code.title: Stored total versus real sum: detect drift
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, StoredTotal REAL);       -- denormalized copy
CREATE TABLE OrderLines (OrderId INTEGER, Qty INTEGER, Price REAL);
INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (1, 30.0), (2, 50.0), (3, 12.0);
INSERT INTO OrderLines VALUES (1, 2, 10.0), (1, 1, 10.0),             -- order 1 = 30
                              (2, 1, 20.0), (2, 1, 25.0),             -- order 2 = 45 (drifted)
                              (3, 3, 4.0);                            -- order 3 = 12
""")
print("Orders (stored totals):", db.execute("SELECT * FROM Orders").fetchall())

# Compare the stored value with the real sum; any row returned has drifted
rows = db.execute("""
    SELECT o.Id, o.StoredTotal, SUM(l.Qty * l.Price) AS RealTotal
    FROM Orders o JOIN OrderLines l ON l.OrderId = o.Id
    GROUP BY o.Id, o.StoredTotal
    HAVING ABS(o.StoredTotal - SUM(l.Qty * l.Price)) > 0.005
""").fetchall()
print("Drifted orders (id, stored, real):", rows)
# Time O(n) over the line rows, extra space O(orders). Run it as a nightly check.

followUps:
An indexed view is a view that has a unique clustered index, so SQL Server stores its result on disk and keeps it up to date automatically. It is a built-in, safe form of denormalization.

Limits: it needs WITH SCHEMABINDING, two-part table names, no outer joins, no MIN/MAX, no subqueries or DISTINCT, and COUNT_BIG(*) is required with GROUP BY. Every write to the base tables must also update the view, so heavy-write tables slow down. Standard edition may not match it automatically unless you use NOEXPAND.

A star schema deliberately repeats descriptive data so reporting queries need few joins: one central fact table surrounded by flat dimension tables.

Example: FactSales(DateKey, ProductKey, StoreKey, Qty, Amount) joins to DimProduct, which holds Product, Category and Brand in one row, even though Category repeats across thousands of products. That repetition is accepted because the data is loaded in batches and rarely updated, so anomalies are easy to control and scans and group-bys get faster.

Run a reconciliation query that recomputes the real value and compares it with the stored one; any mismatch is drift. A scheduled job or a test can do it.

Example: SELECT o.Id FROM Orders o JOIN (SELECT OrderId, SUM(Qty*Price) T FROM OrderLines GROUP BY OrderId) l ON l.OrderId=o.Id WHERE o.Total <> l.T. Alert when it returns rows, and fix the cause (a missed code path or a direct SQL update). Where possible, keep the total correct through one place only, such as a trigger or the single service method that writes lines.

code.title: Same query with and without an index (query plan)
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, CustomerId INTEGER, Total REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (?,?,?)",
               [(i, i % 1000, i * 1.5) for i in range(1, 20001)])   # 20,000 rows
query = "SELECT Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 42"

def plan(label):
    steps = db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + query).fetchall()
    print(label, "->", steps[0][3])

plan("no index  ")                       # full table scan: reads every row, O(n)
db.execute("CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_CustomerId ON Orders(CustomerId)")
plan("with index")                       # B-tree search: O(log n) plus matching rows
print("rows found:", len(db.execute(query).fetchall()))
# Trade-off: every INSERT/UPDATE must now also maintain the index, and it costs extra space O(n).

followUps:
About 4 levels for a billion rows, so a seek reads only about 4 pages.

A page holds 8 KB. For a 4 byte int key, one non-leaf page holds roughly 500 entries (key plus pointer). Then 500 x 500 x 500 = 125 million, and 500^4 = 62 billion. So root, two intermediate levels and the leaf level cover a billion rows. With wide keys (say 100 bytes, about 70 per page) it is closer to 5 levels. This is why seeks stay fast even on huge tables.

Selectivity is the fraction of rows a value picks out: few matching rows means high selectivity, which means an index helps.

Example: in a table of 1,000,000 orders, OrderNumber = 'A123' returns 1 row, so an index is excellent. IsDeleted = 0 returns 950,000 rows; the optimizer will scan instead, because thousands of key lookups cost more than reading the table once. Low-selectivity columns work only as a later column in a composite index or in a filtered index.

Use the usage statistics DMV and compare reads to writes: an index with many updates and almost no seeks or scans is a candidate to drop.

SELECT i.name, s.user_seeks, s.user_scans, s.user_lookups, s.user_updates FROM sys.indexes i LEFT JOIN sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats s ON s.object_id=i.object_id AND s.index_id=i.index_id AND s.database_id=DB_ID(). The counters reset when the server restarts, so only trust them after a full business cycle (including month end). Disable first, then drop later.

Cluster on another column when most queries range over it, or when it gives a narrow, ever-increasing key, for example a date or a tenant plus date.

Example: a table Events with a GUID primary key but nearly every query is WHERE EventDate BETWEEN .... Cluster on (EventDate, Id) and keep the GUID primary key as a nonclustered key. Warning: every other index stores the clustered key, so a wide clustered key makes them all bigger.

A heap is a table with no clustered index: rows are stored in no particular order. It is acceptable for fast bulk-loaded staging tables that are read once, then emptied.

Reasons to avoid heaps otherwise: lookups use a row id (RID), updates that grow a row create forwarded records, and space freed by deletes is not always reused. Example: loading 10 million rows into a staging heap, then moving them to the real table, is a good use. For anything queried repeatedly, add a clustered index.

Changing the clustered key forces every nonclustered index to be rebuilt, because each of them stores the clustered key as its row locator.

Example: a table with 6 nonclustered indexes. Dropping the clustered primary key and re-creating the table clustered on (CustomerId, Id) rewrites the whole table plus all 6 indexes, which can take long and bloat the log. That is why you choose the clustered key carefully up front: narrow, unique, static and ever-increasing.

code.title: Covering index: query answered from the index alone
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, CustomerId INTEGER, Status TEXT, Total REAL, Notes TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)",
               [(i, i % 500, "open", i * 2.0, "x" * 50) for i in range(1, 10001)])
query = "SELECT Total FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 7"

def plan(label):
    print(label, "->", db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + query).fetchone()[3])

db.execute("CREATE INDEX IX_Cust ON Orders(CustomerId)")
plan("key only          ")                # finds rows, then looks each one up in the table
db.execute("DROP INDEX IX_Cust")
db.execute("CREATE INDEX IX_Cust_Total ON Orders(CustomerId, Total)")  # the extra column rides along
plan("with Total in index")               # COVERING INDEX: no trip back to the table
# SQL Server equivalent: CREATE INDEX ... ON Orders(CustomerId) INCLUDE (Total)
# Seek is O(log n); covering removes the extra lookup per row. Space: one more column per index row.

followUps:
Open the actual execution plan and look for a Key Lookup (or RID Lookup) operator next to an Index Seek; it means the index did not cover the query.

Hover the lookup to see the Output List: these are the columns missing from the index. Add them to INCLUDE. Also check Number of Executions: if the seek returned 20,000 rows, the lookup ran 20,000 times, which is where the cost hides. SET STATISTICS IO ON shows the logical reads fall after the fix.

A wide INCLUDE list makes the index nearly a second copy of the table: more disk, more memory, and slower writes.

Every insert, delete, or update of an included column must also change each index that carries it. Example: including a 4000 character Notes column in three indexes on a 10 million row table adds tens of GB. Include only the few small columns the hot queries need, and avoid MAX types.

A filtered index is an index with a WHERE clause, so it holds only the rows you care about. It is smaller and cheaper to maintain.

Example: CREATE INDEX IX_Open ON Orders(CustomerId) WHERE Status = 'Open' when only 2% of 50 million orders are open. Queries must include a matching predicate (and parameterized queries sometimes cannot use it). It is also useful for a unique rule on part of the data, such as unique email where IsDeleted = 0.

code.title: Composite index column order decides which queries it serves
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, CustomerId INTEGER, Status INTEGER, Total REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
               [(i, i % 300, i % 5, i * 1.0) for i in range(1, 15001)])
db.execute("CREATE INDEX IX_Cust_Status ON Orders(CustomerId, Status)")   # equality column first

def plan(sql):
    print(sql, "\n   ->", db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql).fetchone()[3])

plan("SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 5 AND Status = 2")   # uses both columns
plan("SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE CustomerId = 5")                  # uses the leading column
plan("SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE Status = 2")                      # skips the leading column: scan
# Rule: equality columns first, then the range or sort column; the leftmost prefix is what is searchable.
# Seek O(log n) when the leading column is in the filter; otherwise O(n).

followUps:
Yes: one index on (CustomerId, OrderDate) serves any query that filters on CustomerId alone, and queries that filter CustomerId plus a date range.

It does not serve a query on OrderDate alone. So instead of three separate indexes for CustomerId, CustomerId + OrderDate, and so on, one composite covers the first two. Fewer indexes means cheaper writes. It can also serve ORDER BY OrderDate for one customer without a sort.

No. Columns in INCLUDE are only stored at the leaf level to avoid lookups; they are not part of the sort order or the search key, so their order is irrelevant.

Example: INDEX (CustomerId) INCLUDE (Total, Status) is identical to INCLUDE (Status, Total). Order only matters for the key columns, which define how the B-tree is sorted and where a seek can start.

Index intersection means the engine uses two single-column indexes and joins their results to find rows matching both conditions. SQL Server can do it but rarely chooses to, and it is usually slower than one composite index.

Example: indexes on CustomerId and on Status; the plan seeks both, then hash-joins the row ids, then still does key lookups. One composite index (CustomerId, Status) finds the rows in a single seek. So design composite indexes for your real queries.

code.title: Sargable versus non-sargable predicate
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, OrderDate TEXT, Total REAL)")
rows = [(i, "2025-%02d-%02d" % (1 + i % 12, 1 + i % 28), i * 1.0) for i in range(1, 20001)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (?,?,?)", rows)
db.execute("CREATE INDEX IX_Date ON Orders(OrderDate)")

def plan(label, sql):
    print(label, "->", db.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql).fetchone()[3])

# Wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index, so every row is read
plan("non-sargable", "SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE substr(OrderDate, 1, 7) = '2025-03'")
# A plain range on the bare column lets the index jump straight to the start
plan("sargable    ", "SELECT * FROM Orders WHERE OrderDate >= '2025-03-01' AND OrderDate < '2025-04-01'")
# SQL Server: avoid YEAR(OrderDate)=2025, LEFT(Name,3)='Smi', Col+1=5, LIKE '%x'
# Non-sargable is O(n); sargable is O(log n + matches).

followUps:
A leading-wildcard search like LIKE '%phone%' cannot use a normal index, so use full-text search or a trigram-style approach instead.

In SQL Server create a full-text index and query with CONTAINS(Name, '"phone*"') (prefix) or FREETEXT. For rich search at scale, use Azure AI Search or Elasticsearch. If users only need prefix matching, LIKE 'phone%' is sargable and fast. Mind that CONTAINS does not support a leading wildcard either.

A computed column is a column defined by an expression over other columns. Indexing it makes an otherwise non-sargable expression searchable.

Example: instead of WHERE YEAR(OrderDate) = 2025, add OrderYear AS YEAR(OrderDate) PERSISTED and CREATE INDEX IX_Year ON Orders(OrderYear). The expression must be deterministic. In EF Core map it with HasComputedColumnSql("YEAR([OrderDate])"). Often a plain date range is simpler and needs no extra column.

Look in the execution plan for a warning icon on the operator and a CONVERT_IMPLICIT in the predicate; the plan XML shows it under PlanAffectingConvert.

Typical cause: comparing a varchar column with an nvarchar parameter. SQL Server converts the column side, so the index becomes a scan. EF Core maps string to nvarchar by default; call IsUnicode(false) for varchar columns, and make parameter types match column types.

A RID lookup is the same as a key lookup, but for a heap: the nonclustered index holds a row identifier (file, page, slot) instead of a clustered key, and the engine jumps straight to that physical location.

It appears in the plan as RID Lookup (Heap). It is a little cheaper per row than a key lookup, but the same problem exists: 10,000 matching rows means 10,000 separate page reads. Fix by covering the query or by adding a clustered index.

There are three: nested loops, hash match and merge join. The optimizer picks by row counts and sort order.

  • Nested loops: for each outer row, seek the inner side. Best when the outer input is small and the inner side is indexed (10 rows joining a 10 million row table).
  • Merge join: walks two inputs already sorted on the join key. Great for large sorted inputs.
  • Hash match: builds a hash table of the smaller input. Best for big, unsorted, unindexed joins; needs memory and can spill to tempdb.

The optimizer is cost-based and may decide your index is not worth using. Common reasons are below.

  • The predicate is not sargable, or has an implicit conversion.
  • The filter returns too many rows (for example 20% of the table), so a scan is cheaper.
  • The index is not covering and key lookups would cost more.
  • Statistics are stale, so the row estimate is wrong.
  • The leading column of the index is not in the query.

Check the actual plan and compare estimated with actual rows.

The estimated plan is what the optimizer expects before running the query; the actual plan includes what really happened (actual rows, executions, spills, warnings).

Compare Estimated Number of Rows with Actual Number of Rows: if the estimate is 10 and the actual is 2,000,000, the plan was built on a wrong guess, and statistics or sniffing are the usual suspects. The estimated plan is safe on production because it does not execute the query.

Then the time is probably being spent outside the operators you are looking at: waiting, blocking, or returning data.

  • Blocking or locks: check sys.dm_exec_requests wait types.
  • Parameter sniffing: the plan suits other values.
  • Huge result set or slow client reading it (ASYNC_NETWORK_IO).
  • Memory grant waits or tempdb spills.
  • A scalar function or trigger not obvious in the plan.

Wait statistics tell you which one.

Query Store keeps the history of plans and runtimes per query, so you can see exactly which query got slower and what plan it used before the deployment.

Open Regressed Queries, find the query whose duration jumped, compare the old and new plan, and if the old plan was better use Force Plan as an immediate fix while you correct the root cause. It is on by default in new SQL Server 2022 and Azure SQL databases. Forcing is a patch: unforce when the code is fixed.

code.title: Parameter sniffing: a cached plan built for the first value

followUps:
Usually because SSMS and the app use different session SET options (most often ARITHABORT), so each gets its own cached plan, and the app's plan was sniffed for an unlucky value.

You test in SSMS with a literal or fresh plan and it is fast; the app reuses a bad cached plan and is slow. To reproduce, match the SET options or look up the app's plan in Query Store. Clearing that plan (sp_recompile) makes the app fast again, which proves sniffing.

At 500 executions per second it is expensive: every run pays a full compile, burning CPU and taking compile locks.

If a compile takes 5 ms of CPU, 500 per second is 2.5 CPU seconds each second, which is two to three cores gone. Use RECOMPILE only for queries that run rarely and are heavily skewed. For hot queries prefer OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN, two separate code paths for big and small values, or a better index. Newer SQL Server versions also have Parameter Sensitive Plan optimization.

Yes. EF Core sends parameterized SQL (sp_executesql), so the plan is sniffed in exactly the same way.

A query like Where(o => o.CustomerId == id) becomes WHERE CustomerId = @p0 and the first value compiles the plan for everyone. Note that values captured as constants in the expression are parameterized, but EF Core can also inline literal values written in the query. Fixes: query hints via an interceptor, splitting the query, or better statistics.

The ascending key problem happens when new rows are always bigger than the last value in the statistics histogram, so the optimizer thinks nothing exists beyond it and estimates about 1 row.

Example: statistics on OrderDate were last updated yesterday; today's orders have dates beyond the histogram. A query for today estimates 1 row but gets 80,000, so it picks nested loops and runs for minutes. Fixes: update statistics more often on such columns, or rely on the newer cardinality estimator which handles it better.

It depends: a normal rebuild is offline and blocks users, while an online rebuild keeps the table available but needs Enterprise (or Azure SQL / newer editions).

ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON) allows reads and writes, with short locks at the start and end. Resumable rebuilds in SQL Server 2017+ can pause and continue. It still uses extra space, CPU and log, so schedule it in a quiet period.

REORGANIZE tidies the leaf pages in place, a little at a time, and is always online. REBUILD drops and re-creates the index entirely and also refreshes statistics with a full scan.

Common guidance is to reorganize at 5-30% fragmentation and rebuild above 30%, but on SSDs fragmentation matters much less than good statistics. Example: a 40% fragmented index with 100 pages is not worth any effort; one with 1,000,000 pages might be.

code.title: Why random GUID keys cause scattered inserts

followUps:
Because every nonclustered index stores a copy of the clustered key in each row, so a 16 byte GUID is copied into all of them, versus 4 bytes for an int.

Example: 100 million rows with 5 nonclustered indexes. A GUID adds 12 more bytes in each of 6 structures: 12 x 6 x 100 million is about 7 GB extra, which also means less of the index fits in memory. A narrow clustered key keeps everything smaller.

EF Core generates the GUID on the client side, before the insert, using a sequential-friendly algorithm for SQL Server so values increase and avoid random page splits.

You can see this when you declare Guid Id as the key: the SQL Server provider uses SequentialGuidValueGenerator, so inserts are ordered the way SQL Server sorts uniqueidentifier. Because the value is set before saving, you also know the id without a round trip, which helps when inserting parents and children together.

Last-page insert contention is when many sessions insert at once into a table with an ever-increasing clustered key, so all of them fight for the latch on the same last page.

It appears at very high insert rates (thousands per second) as PAGELATCH_EX waits. It is the downside of sequential keys; remedies include OPTIMIZE_FOR_SEQUENTIAL_KEY = ON (SQL Server 2019+), a partitioned or hashed leading column, or batching the inserts.

A columnstore stores data by column, not by row: each column is compressed separately in segments of about a million rows. A B-tree stores whole rows together in sorted pages.

For a report that sums one column of 500 million rows, columnstore reads only that compressed column and uses batch mode, often 10x faster and 5-10x smaller. B-trees win for finding or updating a few rows by key. Updates go to a row-store delta store first, and a background process compresses them.

A nonclustered columnstore on a busy OLTP table adds write overhead and some locking cost, because every insert, update, and delete must also be reflected in the columnstore (delta store and delete bitmap).

Also the columnstore needs maintenance (merging delta stores, removing deleted rows), uses extra memory, and a heavy report can compete with transactions for resources. Keep it to analytic columns, and consider a read replica for reports.

Create it online, in a quiet window, in small steps, and watch the log and blocking.

Use CREATE INDEX ... WITH (ONLINE = ON, RESUMABLE = ON, MAX_DURATION = 60), which can pause and resume. Build it with a limited MAXDOP, ensure there is room in the log and tempdb, and test the same index on a restored copy first for timing. With a partitioned table, you can build per partition. Check the new index is actually used before dropping an old one.

code.title: Transaction atomicity: all or nothing
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)   # we control BEGIN/COMMIT ourselves
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Accounts (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Balance INTEGER CHECK (Balance >= 0))")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Accounts VALUES (?,?)", [(1, 100), (2, 50)])

def balances():
    return db.execute("SELECT Id, Balance FROM Accounts ORDER BY Id").fetchall()

def transfer(src, dst, amount):
    db.execute("BEGIN")
    try:
        db.execute("UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - ? WHERE Id = ?", (amount, src))
        db.execute("UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + ? WHERE Id = ?", (amount, dst))
        db.execute("COMMIT")            # both updates become permanent together
        print("transfer", amount, "ok:", balances())
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
        db.execute("ROLLBACK")          # the half-done first update is undone
        print("transfer", amount, "failed (" + str(e) + "), rolled back:", balances())

print("start:", balances())
transfer(1, 2, 30)     # fine
transfer(1, 2, 500)    # CHECK constraint breaks on the debit, nothing is kept
# Each transfer is O(1) work; the log gives durability and the rollback.

followUps:
SET XACT_ABORT ON makes SQL Server roll back the whole transaction automatically when any run-time error occurs, instead of continuing with the next statement.

Without it, a failing statement (a constraint violation) may leave the earlier statements committed, giving a half-finished transfer. With it on, the error aborts and rolls back everything, and it also handles client timeouts cleanly. Put it at the top of every stored procedure that has a transaction.

A savepoint is a named marker inside a transaction that lets you roll back part of the work without cancelling the entire transaction.

In T-SQL: SAVE TRANSACTION Step1; then later ROLLBACK TRANSACTION Step1; undoes only what happened after the savepoint; the outer transaction can still commit. Example: an order batch where a bad line is skipped but the 9 good lines are kept. EF Core creates savepoints automatically when SaveChanges runs inside your own transaction.

Because locks are held until the transaction ends, so a long transaction blocks other users and grows the log.

Example: a transaction that updates a row and then waits 5 seconds for an HTTP call keeps that row locked for 5 seconds. At 100 requests per second, requests queue up and deadlocks and timeouts appear. Do the slow work (HTTP, files, user input) outside the transaction, and keep it to the database writes only.

Pass the level when you start the transaction: await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(IsolationLevel.Snapshot), then call SaveChangesAsync and CommitAsync.

Alternatively wrap the code in a TransactionScope with TransactionOptions { IsolationLevel = ... }. EF Core has no per-query isolation setting, apart from hints like WITH (NOLOCK) via an interceptor. Without a transaction of your own, each SaveChanges uses the database default (read committed).

I would use SNAPSHOT isolation, or SERIALIZABLE if snapshot is not available, so every query in the report sees the same point-in-time data.

Snapshot gives a consistent view without blocking writers, which matters during month end. Better still, run the report against a read replica or a restored snapshot. At plain read committed, the report totals can be inconsistent if rows change while it runs.

SERIALIZABLE takes range locks that cover the gaps between keys, and holds them until commit, so many transactions block each other and cycles form more easily.

Example: two transactions both read WHERE CustomerId = 5 (range-locking that range), then both try to insert a row into the same range. Each waits for the other to release the range lock, which is a classic deadlock. Use it only for short critical sections.

A phantom read causes a bug whenever you check a rule over a set of rows and then insert based on it.

Example: a meeting room booking. Transaction A checks that no booking overlaps 10:00-11:00 and finds none. Before it inserts, transaction B inserts a booking for 10:30. Both commit and the room is double booked. Fix with SERIALIZABLE, a unique constraint, or a lock such as UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK on the range.

Use optimistic concurrency: add a rowversion column and make the update conditional on it.

UPDATE Items SET Qty = @q WHERE Id = @id AND RowVersion = @oldVersion; if 0 rows are affected, someone changed the row first, so reload and retry. In EF Core mark the property with [Timestamp] or IsRowVersion(). An atomic update such as SET Qty = Qty - 1 also avoids the lost update entirely.

Under RCSI (read committed snapshot) dirty reads cannot happen, but non-repeatable reads and phantom reads still can.

Each statement sees a snapshot as of when that statement started, so two reads of the same row in one transaction can return different values if another transaction commits in between. Lost updates are also still possible unless you use a rowversion check or higher isolation. Only SNAPSHOT or SERIALIZABLE protect against all three.

Blocking is one session waiting for another that holds a lock; it ends when the holder commits. A deadlock is a cycle where each waits for the other, so it never ends without intervention.

Example: A updates row 1 and waits for row 2 while B holds row 2 and waits for row 1. SQL Server detects the cycle within seconds, kills one session with error 1205, and the other continues. Blocking is a performance problem; a deadlock is an error you must retry.

Query the live requests: SELECT session_id, blocking_session_id, wait_type, wait_time, text FROM sys.dm_exec_requests r CROSS APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(r.sql_handle) WHERE blocking_session_id <> 0.

The row with a blocking_session_id shows the victim; follow the id up to the head blocker, which is the session with no blocker itself. sp_who2 and Activity Monitor show the same. Check what the head blocker is doing (often an open transaction waiting for the client).

UPDLOCK takes update locks on the rows you read, so no one else can lock them for update before you do, but others can still read them.

Use it for a read-then-update pattern: SELECT Qty FROM Stock WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) WHERE Id = 7 then UPDATE. Two sessions doing this queue up politely instead of both taking shared locks and deadlocking on the upgrade. It is a pessimistic technique, so keep the transaction short.

code.title: Deadlock avoided by locking in a fixed order

followUps:
SQL Server picks the session that is cheapest to roll back, based on the amount of log it has written, unless a deadlock priority says otherwise.

The lock monitor runs about every 5 seconds (faster once deadlocks start) looking for cycles. Example: session A has updated 10 rows and B has updated 100,000 rows; A is chosen as the victim and receives error 1205. The application must catch it and retry the whole transaction.

Yes. A SELECT takes shared locks on an index and then needs a key lookup into the clustered index, while an UPDATE locks the clustered row and then the index.

Example: the SELECT holds a shared lock on a nonclustered index row and wants the clustered row; the UPDATE holds the clustered row lock and wants to update the index row. Each waits for the other. The fix is a covering index (no lookup), or row-versioning isolation so readers do not take shared locks.

SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY tells SQL Server which session to sacrifice if a deadlock happens: LOW, NORMAL, HIGH or a number from -10 to 10.

Set a background batch job to LOW so that it is killed instead of a customer-facing request. Example: SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW; at the start of the nightly job. It does not prevent deadlocks, it only controls who loses.

Row versions are kept in the version store in tempdb (or, with Accelerated Database Recovery, in the user database). Old versions are removed when no transaction needs them any more.

The store grows when a transaction stays open for a long time, because versions created after it began cannot be cleaned. Example: a forgotten open transaction for 3 hours on a busy system can fill tempdb with GBs of versions. Monitor sys.dm_tran_version_store_space_usage and the oldest active transaction.

No. RCSI removes most reader-writer blocking, but writers still lock rows, so two sessions updating the same rows in opposite order can still deadlock.

What it removes is the deadlock between a reader and a writer (the SELECT with lookup case). Writer-versus-writer deadlocks need consistent access order or shorter transactions. Also, RCSI is a database-level setting, so it changes behavior for all queries under read committed.

Pick SNAPSHOT when a transaction needs a consistent view of the data across several statements, such as a report that reads three tables. RCSI only gives consistency within each single statement.

SNAPSHOT also raises an update conflict error (3960) if you try to update a row changed since your snapshot began, so you must handle retry. It needs ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON, and you opt in per transaction.

code.title: Optimistic concurrency with a version number

followUps:
You have three options: keep the database values (client loses), keep the client values (overwrite), or merge them. Which one is right is a business decision.

In the catch block, read ex.Entries, call GetDatabaseValuesAsync(), then set OriginalValues to the database values to retry with the client's changes, or reload and show the user both versions. For counters, a retry that recomputes from fresh data is usually correct. Do not retry blindly in a loop.

Use a normal column as the concurrency token, such as LastModified, or all the original values of the row, and compare them in the WHERE clause.

In EF Core mark the property with [ConcurrencyCheck] or .IsConcurrencyToken(). EF then generates WHERE Id = @id AND LastModified = @original. It works, but a rowversion is safer because the database changes it automatically, whereas a datetime can collide when two updates happen in the same tick.

sp_getapplock takes a named, application-level lock that is not tied to any table row, held until the transaction or session ends.

Example: EXEC sp_getapplock @Resource = 'nightly-import', @LockMode = 'Exclusive', @LockTimeout = 0 ensures only one instance of a job runs even when several app servers start it. It returns a code (0 or 1 for success, negative for timeout) that you must check, and works across servers because the lock lives in the database.

code.title: Transactional outbox: save data and message together

followUps:
The consumer records the id of each message it has handled and skips any id it has already seen, ideally in the same transaction as its own change.

Example: a table ProcessedMessages(MessageId PRIMARY KEY). On receipt, insert the id and do the work in one transaction; a duplicate violates the primary key and the work is skipped. Alternatively make the operation naturally idempotent, such as SET Status = 'Reserved' rather than Qty = Qty - 1.

Choose choreography for simple flows with few steps, and orchestration when the flow is long, has branches, or needs a clear owner.

In choreography each service listens for events and reacts, so there is no central brain, but the flow is hard to see. In orchestration one coordinator (for example a Durable Functions orchestrator) calls the steps and handles compensations, so the flow is in one place. With 3 steps I would choreograph; with 8 steps and timeouts I would orchestrate.

Change data capture reads the database transaction log and publishes the committed outbox rows as events, so the app no longer needs a polling loop.

Tools like Debezium (or SQL Server CDC / change tracking feeding a connector) stream new rows to Kafka or Service Bus within milliseconds, with no repeated queries. The cost is more infrastructure to run and monitor, and delivery is still at-least-once, so the consumer must stay idempotent.

Call it with FromSql: db.Orders.FromSql($"EXEC GetOrders {customerId}").ToListAsync(). It returns entities or keyless types, and the interpolated value becomes a parameter.

For procedures that do not return rows, use db.Database.ExecuteSqlAsync($"EXEC Archive {date}"). Results of FromSql cannot be composed with further LINQ that needs SQL on top of an EXEC (the stored procedure cannot be wrapped in a subquery). From EF Core 7 you can also map insert, update and delete to procedures.

Keep them in source control and deploy them through the same pipeline as the app, ideally as migrations or with a tool such as a SQL project (dacpac).

Rule of thumb: the procedure version must be compatible with both the old and the new app version during a rolling deployment, so add new optional parameters with defaults instead of changing signatures. Use CREATE OR ALTER in repeatable scripts, and tests on a real database in CI.

Stored procedures are better at set-based, data-heavy work that is much faster close to the data, and at security by permission on the procedure alone.

Example: a month-end job that updates 5 million rows with several joins and a temp table runs in the database with no network round trips. Also a procedure can be tuned or fixed without redeploying the app. LINQ is better for ordinary CRUD, composable queries and refactoring safety.

Find(id) looks in the tracked entities first and queries only if it is not there; First returns the first match and fails if none; Single expects exactly one and throws if there are zero or more than one.

Use Find only for primary key lookups. Use FirstOrDefault with an order for the latest item. Use Single when a duplicate would be a bug. Single costs a TOP 2 query so it can detect the extra row.

Often not: DbContext already implements the repository and unit of work patterns, so a thin generic wrapper adds code without value.

A repository is still useful when it hides complex queries behind meaningful names (GetOverdueInvoices), or when you want to unit test business logic without EF. Avoid a generic IRepository<T> that only forwards Add and Find, and avoid returning IQueryable from it.

OnModelCreating is where you configure the model with the Fluent API: keys, relationships, column types, indexes, and seed data.

Example: modelBuilder.Entity<Order>().HasIndex(o => o.CustomerId); modelBuilder.Entity<Order>().Property(o => o.Total).HasPrecision(18, 2);. Fluent API wins over attributes, and for larger models you split the code into IEntityTypeConfiguration<T> classes and call ApplyConfigurationsFromAssembly.

code.title: SQL injection versus a parameterized query
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Users (Name TEXT, Secret TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Users VALUES (?,?)", [("ann", "s1"), ("bob", "s2"), ("cy", "s3")])

attack = "x' OR '1'='1"       # what a malicious user types into the name box
print("input:", attack)

# Vulnerable: the input is glued into the SQL text, so it changes the query's meaning
bad_sql = "SELECT Name, Secret FROM Users WHERE Name = '" + attack + "'"
print("concatenated:", db.execute(bad_sql).fetchall())

# Safe: the input travels as a parameter and is always treated as a value
print("parameterized:", db.execute("SELECT Name, Secret FROM Users WHERE Name = ?", (attack,)).fetchall())

# In .NET: SqlParameter / EF Core FromSql($"... {value}") / Dapper @param, never string +.
# Time O(n) scan here, space O(1).

followUps:
No. A procedure is safe only if it uses parameters; if it builds a string inside and runs it with EXEC(@sql), the injection happens inside the procedure.

Example: EXEC('SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = ''' + @name + '''') is just as vulnerable. Use sp_executesql with typed parameters and QUOTENAME for identifiers. Also, the app must call the procedure with parameters, not by concatenating the EXEC text.

In EF Core 8+ FromSql takes an interpolated string and turns each value into a parameter, so it is safe. FromSqlRaw takes a plain string you build yourself, so it is only safe if you pass parameters explicitly.

Example: FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Users WHERE Name = {name}") is parameterized. FromSqlRaw($"... {name}") is injectable, because the string was already interpolated before EF saw it. Prefer FromSql.

Never put the user's text in the SQL. Map the allowed choices to a whitelist of known column names and use only the mapped value.

Example: var col = sort switch { "name" => "Name", "date" => "CreatedAt", _ => "Id" }; then build the ORDER BY from col. With LINQ, pick between two lambdas such as OrderBy(x => x.Name). Parameters cannot be used for column names, so the whitelist is the only safe way.

code.title: Change tracking by comparing against a snapshot

followUps:
Attach starts tracking an entity as Unchanged; Update starts tracking it as Modified and marks all its properties as changed.

Example: you get a Customer from a request. Update(c) sends an UPDATE for every column, even those that did not change. Attach(c) and then setting Entry(c).Property(x => x.City).IsModified = true updates only the City column. If the key is unset, Update treats the entity as new (Added).

Override SaveChanges (or use a SaveChangesInterceptor) and loop over ChangeTracker.Entries() to set the values for all added and modified entities.

Short fragment:

foreach (var e in ChangeTracker.Entries<IAuditable>())
  if (e.State == EntityState.Modified) {
    e.Entity.ModifiedAt = now; e.Entity.ModifiedBy = user; }

Get the user from an injected service, not a static. An interceptor keeps the logic out of the context class.

It turns off the automatic scan for property changes that EF normally runs before queries, SaveChanges and similar calls. It is useful when you add or change a huge number of entities.

Example: inserting 100,000 entities in a loop, where each Add would otherwise re-scan the tracked set, giving O(n squared) behavior. Disable it, do the work, and then call ChangeTracker.DetectChanges() once. The risk: if you change a property and forget to detect, the change is silently not saved.

You get an InvalidOperationException saying that a second operation was started on this context instance before a previous operation completed. Sometimes you get odd errors from the data reader instead.

It usually comes from forgetting an await, from running Task.WhenAll over queries on one context, or from storing a context in a singleton. Fix: one context per unit of work, or create a new one per parallel task from IDbContextFactory<T>.

With pooling, an instance is reset and reused instead of created for each request, so it must carry no per-request state.

Do not keep request data (the current tenant or user) in fields of the context, because the next request would see it. Inject such values through a scoped service read when needed, or use the pooled factory with care. Constructor-injected scoped services are not supported in pooled contexts. Pooling helps only when context creation shows up in profiles.

Hosted services are singletons, so inject IDbContextFactory<AppDb> or IServiceScopeFactory and create a scope for each unit of work.

using var scope = scopeFactory.CreateScope();
var db = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDb>();
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);

Never inject the scoped context straight into the hosted service constructor: it would live forever, grow its change tracker, and fail on the first concurrent use.

You create a new migration that reverses the change (the safe way), or you apply the previous migration's Down code with dotnet ef database update PreviousMigration if no data would be lost.

In production, rolling forward is usually safer: write a new migration that fixes the problem, because Down for a dropped column cannot bring the data back. That is why destructive changes should happen in a later release, after the code stopped using the column, and with a backup. Test the Down script on a copy first.

Both migrations are valid, but the model snapshot file (ModelSnapshot.cs) conflicts in source control, and the second migration was generated without knowing about the first.

Fix: resolve the snapshot merge, then remove and re-create one of the migrations (dotnet ef migrations remove, then add again) so that it is built on top of the other. Never edit migration timestamps by hand. Small, frequent merges reduce the pain.

Use HasData() in the model for small, static reference data, or a hand-written SQL MERGE in a migration (or an idempotent startup seeder) for data that must be kept in sync.

From EF Core 9 there is also UseSeeding and UseAsyncSeeding to seed through code. Give each seed row an explicit key. For large or environment-specific data, use a deployment script, not a migration.

code.title: The N+1 query problem versus one batched query

followUps:
Yes: an Include of a collection joins parent and children into one result, so the parent columns are repeated for every child (a cartesian explosion).

Example: 100 orders each with 50 lines and 20 payments, with two collection Includes, returns 100 x 50 x 20 = 100,000 rows with duplicated order data. Fixes: AsSplitQuery(), project only needed columns with Select, or include only one collection per query.

Load the orders in the first query, then load the related rows with a second query that uses the order ids, or use AsSplitQuery().

var orders = await db.Orders.Where(...).Take(50).ToListAsync();
var ids = orders.Select(o => o.Id).ToList();
var lines = await db.Lines.Where(l => ids.Contains(l.OrderId)).ToListAsync();

With the context tracking, EF fixes up the navigation properties, so order.Lines is filled with no extra queries.

Count the queries in a test: capture the SQL using a logger or a DbCommandInterceptor that increments a counter, then assert the count.

Example: in an integration test call the endpoint with 50 orders and Assert.True(counter.Count <= 3). With 1 query before the fix and 51 after a regression, the test fails at once. Run it against a real or Testcontainers database so the query shape is genuine.

Lazy loading hits the database on first access of a navigation property, which can happen inside the JSON serializer, one query per object, long after your service finished.

Returning 100 orders and serializing them touches order.Customer and order.Lines for each, giving hundreds of queries, possible exceptions if the context is already disposed, and even circular reference loops. Return DTOs built by a projection, not entities, and keep lazy loading turned off.

A filtered Include restricts which related rows are loaded: Include(o => o.Lines.Where(l => !l.IsCancelled).OrderBy(l => l.LineNo).Take(5)).

It works for collection navigations and supports Where, OrderBy, Skip and Take. The filter is applied in SQL, so only the matching children come back. Caveat: if the same entity was loaded earlier in the same tracked context with an unfiltered Include, the collection can contain more items than your filter, because the tracker fixes up all known rows.

A single query is better when the child collections are small, when you need the data to be consistent at one instant, or when joining returns few extra duplicates.

Split queries run several statements, so data can change between them and you may see an inconsistent graph unless you use a snapshot transaction. They also add round trips. Use split for large collections with several Includes, and single for one small collection.

code.title: Deferred execution: where the filter runs

followUps:
It executes when you enumerate it: ToList(), ToArray(), foreach, First(), Single(), Count(), Any() and so on.

Building it with Where, OrderBy, Select only changes the expression tree. Enumerating twice runs the SQL twice, so store the result with ToList when you reuse it. In EF Core also await ...ToListAsync() and FirstOrDefaultAsync().

It sends a query that loads the whole table into memory, and then Where filters it in the application using LINQ to Objects.

Example: a table with 5 million orders and ToList().Where(o => o.Id == 7) transfers 5 million rows to find 1. Memory spikes and the request is very slow. Always put Where, OrderBy and Select before ToList so they translate into SQL.

For: callers can compose their own filters, sorting and paging, so you write fewer repository methods. Against: it leaks the ORM, the query runs later (maybe after the context is disposed), and callers can build slow or untestable queries.

I prefer returning materialized results or DTOs from named methods, because the query shape is then controlled and testable. An IQueryable is fine inside one layer, for example inside the data access project where the context lives.

Attach it and mark the changed properties: db.Attach(entity); db.Entry(entity).Property(x => x.Name).IsModified = true;, or call Update(entity) to update every column.

You can also simply re-query it with tracking, change it, and save. Another option is ExecuteUpdateAsync, which needs no loaded entity. Remember that no-tracking entities do not detect changes, so setting properties alone does nothing.

Identity resolution means that when the same row appears several times in a tracked query, EF returns one shared object instance rather than several copies.

With AsNoTracking EF creates a separate object for each occurrence, e.g. 100 orders of one customer give 100 different customer objects (more memory). If you want sharing without tracking, use AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution(), which is slower but keeps one instance per key.

Set it in the context: ChangeTracker.QueryTrackingBehavior = QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking in the constructor, or UseQueryTrackingBehavior(...) in the options.

Then use AsTracking() on queries that will be updated. This is a good default for read-heavy APIs, since most requests only read. Be careful that code relying on tracking (loading an entity and changing it) will silently stop saving.

A value converter changes a .NET value into a database value and back. Use it for enums as strings, strongly typed ids, or custom types.

Example: builder.Property(o => o.Status).HasConversion<string>() stores the enum name "Shipped" instead of the number 2. Or store a Money struct as a decimal. Converters can prevent translation of some comparisons, so test the generated SQL.

Since EF Core 5, two collection navigations on each side are enough: EF creates the join table for you.

Example: class Student { public List<Course> Courses { get; } } and class Course { public List<Student> Students { get; } }, with HasMany(s => s.Courses).WithMany(c => c.Students). If the link needs extra data (enrolled date, grade), make an explicit join entity instead.

A compiled query is a LINQ query translated once and cached as a delegate, so repeated calls skip the translation step: EF.CompileAsyncQuery((AppDb db, int id) => db.Orders.First(o => o.Id == id)).

EF already caches query translations, so the gain is small, a few microseconds per call. It matters only for very hot paths, executing thousands of times per second, after profiling shows translation overhead.

code.title: Deleting a large table in batches
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Logs (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Age INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Logs VALUES (?,?)", [(i, i % 100) for i in range(1, 10001)])
print("rows before:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Logs").fetchone()[0])

batch_size = 1500
batches = 0
while True:
    # One short statement per batch keeps locks and the transaction log small
    # (SQL Server: DELETE TOP (1500) FROM Logs WHERE Age >= 50, or EF Core ExecuteDeleteAsync in a loop)
    cur = db.execute("DELETE FROM Logs WHERE Id IN (SELECT Id FROM Logs WHERE Age >= 50 LIMIT ?)",
                     (batch_size,))
    db.commit()
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        break
    batches += 1
    print("batch", batches, "deleted", cur.rowcount)

print("rows after:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Logs").fetchone()[0])
# Total work O(n); each batch holds locks only briefly, and memory stays O(batch size).

followUps:
One huge DELETE holds locks on millions of rows, can escalate to a table lock that blocks everyone, and fills the transaction log; if it fails near the end, the rollback takes as long again.

Deleting 5,000 rows at a time commits quickly, keeps locks short, lets the log be reused (in simple recovery) or backed up, and can be paused. Pause briefly between batches if replication or an availability group is lagging.

They do not get set automatically, because ExecuteUpdate goes straight to SQL and skips the change tracker and SaveChanges interceptors.

Include them in the call: .ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(x => x.Status, "Closed").SetProperty(x => x.ModifiedAt, now)). Wrap it in a small helper if many call sites need it. A database trigger or a default would also work but is less visible.

A table-valued parameter (TVP) lets you pass a whole table of rows, as one parameter, to a stored procedure or query.

Example: send 10,000 ids as a TVP of type dbo.IdList and join to it, instead of a huge IN (...) list or 10,000 calls. It is typed, avoids plan-cache bloat from different list sizes, and works well with MERGE. In ADO.NET use SqlDbType.Structured; Dapper supports it through DataTable.

code.title: Keyset (seek) pagination versus OFFSET
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Orders (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Total REAL)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Orders VALUES (?,?)", [(i, i * 1.5) for i in range(1, 10001)])
page_size = 5

# OFFSET: the engine must walk and discard the first 9,990 rows before it returns 5
offset_rows = db.execute("SELECT Id FROM Orders ORDER BY Id LIMIT ? OFFSET ?", (page_size, 9990)).fetchall()
print("OFFSET page:", [r[0] for r in offset_rows])

# Keyset: remember the last Id from the previous page and seek straight to it using the index
last_seen_id = 9990
keyset_rows = db.execute("SELECT Id FROM Orders WHERE Id > ? ORDER BY Id LIMIT ?", (last_seen_id, page_size)).fetchall()
print("keyset page:", [r[0] for r in keyset_rows])
print("same result:", offset_rows == keyset_rows)
# OFFSET cost grows with the page number: O(offset + page). Keyset is O(log n + page) on any page.

followUps:
Keyset pagination fetches the next page with WHERE Id > @lastId ORDER BY Id, so the index seeks directly to the place; OFFSET must read and throw away all earlier rows.

Page 10,000 with OFFSET reads 100,000 rows to return 10; keyset reads about 10. Drawbacks: no jump to arbitrary page number, and the sort needs a unique tie-breaker (for example (CreatedAt, Id)). It is ideal for infinite scroll and APIs.

A compiled query is worth it only for hot paths, thousands of calls per second, and after profiling shows query translation in the top costs.

For the typical endpoint the database time (milliseconds) dwarfs the microseconds saved. Fix indexes, round trips and over-fetching first. Compiled queries also make code less readable and they cannot be composed afterwards.

Add a test that counts queries and asserts a budget, track durations in Application Insights, and review slow queries regularly in Query Store.

Example: an integration test that calls the endpoint and asserts at most 3 SQL commands. In production, alert when the p95 of the endpoint, or the database duration for that query, grows above a threshold. Run load tests with realistic data volumes, because small test data hides missing indexes.

Use Dapper and EF Core in the same DbConnection and DbTransaction: let EF open the transaction, then give Dapper its connection and transaction.

await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();
var conn = db.Database.GetDbConnection();
await conn.ExecuteAsync(sql, args, tx.GetDbTransaction());
await db.SaveChangesAsync(); await tx.CommitAsync();

Both then see each other's uncommitted changes and commit or roll back together.

You use the splitOn overload of QueryAsync with a function that builds the parent and attaches the children, and group by parent id yourself.

Example: QueryAsync<Order, Line, Order>(sql, (o, l) => { cache.TryAdd(o.Id, o); cache[o.Id].Lines.Add(l); return cache[o.Id]; }, splitOn: "LineId"). The join repeats the order row per line, so de-duplicate with a dictionary. For two or three levels, QueryMultiple with separate result sets is often simpler.

Keep SQL in named files or constants close to the data access class, use parameters only, and test every query against a real database in CI.

Use integration tests with a container (Testcontainers) that run each query with sample data and assert the shape of the result. Put complex queries in views or stored procedures under source control. Name columns explicitly (no SELECT *) so a schema change fails a test, not production.

code.title: Expand and contract: rename a column without downtime
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE Customers (Id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, Surname TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (?,?)", [(i, "name%d" % i) for i in range(1, 11)])

# Step 1 EXPAND: add the new column; old code keeps working because nothing was removed
db.execute("ALTER TABLE Customers ADD COLUMN LastName TEXT")

# Step 2 BACKFILL in small batches so locks stay short (new code also writes both columns)
total = 0
while True:
    cur = db.execute("UPDATE Customers SET LastName = Surname WHERE Id IN "
                     "(SELECT Id FROM Customers WHERE LastName IS NULL LIMIT 4)")
    db.commit()
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        break
    total += cur.rowcount
    print("backfilled batch of", cur.rowcount)

# Step 3 VERIFY before the switch: no row may differ
missing = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Customers WHERE LastName IS NULL OR LastName <> Surname").fetchone()[0]
print("rows backfilled:", total, "| mismatches:", missing)

# Step 4 CONTRACT: later release, once no code reads the old column
if missing == 0:
    db.execute("ALTER TABLE Customers DROP COLUMN Surname")
print("final columns:", [c[1] for c in db.execute("PRAGMA table_info(Customers)")])
# Backfill is O(n) in small batches; no step takes a long exclusive lock.

followUps:
Adding a nullable column, or a NOT NULL column with a constant default, is a metadata-only change on current SQL Server (Enterprise and since 2012, in all editions for runtime constants), so it is instant. A default that is non-deterministic, or an older version, forces SQL Server to write the value to every row.

Example: ALTER TABLE T ADD Flag bit NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 on 100 million rows is instant, while adding a column with DEFAULT NEWID() rewrites every row and holds a schema lock. Always test the time on production-sized data.

Split the work into several migrations across releases: one adds the new column, application code writes both, a data migration copies old to new in batches, and a later migration drops the old column.

In EF Core, use migrationBuilder.AddColumn and migrationBuilder.Sql("UPDATE ... batch") or run the backfill as a background job. Be careful: RenameColumn is a single step that breaks the old app version during a rolling deployment, so avoid it on large live tables.

Compare counts and checksums between old and new columns with queries, and run them until they come back clean.

Examples: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM T WHERE New IS NULL OR New <> Old must return 0; SELECT CHECKSUM_AGG(CHECKSUM(Old)), CHECKSUM_AGG(CHECKSUM(New)) should match. Also check rows written during the backfill, since new code writes both columns. Only after a clean run for a full business cycle should you drop the old column.

It means the database does not enforce a schema, but your code still assumes one: every reader must cope with missing fields, different types and old shapes.

Example: documents written last year have fullName and new ones have firstName and lastName. Every reader must handle both, or you migrate the old ones. The schema moved from the database into the application, so you need versioned documents, validation on write and tests.

The CAP theorem says that during a network partition a distributed system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets an answer).

Partitions do happen, so the practical choice is CP (refuse or delay some requests to stay correct) or AP (always answer, maybe with stale data). A single-node SQL Server is not affected in the same way. PACELC adds that even without a partition you trade latency against consistency.

An e-commerce system: SQL Server holds orders and payments, which need transactions, and Cosmos DB or a search index holds a denormalized product catalogue for fast reads.

Another example is Redis for a session cache beside SQL for the data. The risk is keeping them in sync, so choose one system of record and feed the other through events (outbox plus a change feed). Do not write to both inside one request and hope.

Use provisioned throughput for steady, predictable load, autoscale for variable load with clear peaks, and serverless for small or sporadic workloads.

Provisioned: you pay for a fixed number of RU/s every hour (cheapest if well used). Autoscale: scales between 10% and 100% of a maximum, and the rate is about 1.5x per RU. Serverless: pay per RU consumed, with limits on size and throughput, ideal for dev/test. Check current limits in the Azure docs.

A logical partition is all the items that share one partition key value (limited to 20 GB). A physical partition is the server-side storage and compute unit that hosts many logical partitions.

You choose the key, so you control the logical partitions; Azure decides the physical placement and splits them as data grows (each physical partition holds up to about 50 GB and 10,000 RU/s). A hot logical partition cannot spread over several physical ones.

Read the request charge from the response: the SDK exposes response.RequestCharge (or the x-ms-request-charge header) for every operation.

Example: a point read of a 1 KB item costs about 1 RU; a cross-partition query might cost 50 RU. Log the charge in development and for the heaviest queries in production. The Azure portal Data Explorer also shows the Query Stats with RU for each query.

code.title: Partition key choice and skew

followUps:
You cannot change the partition key of an existing container; you create a new container with the right key and copy the data over.

Use the Cosmos DB container copy job or a migration with the change feed processor, dual-write during the switch, and then cut over. Plan for the extra RU/s and storage while both exist. Choose the key carefully at the start, because this is a heavy operation. (Hierarchical partition keys can help with some skew without a full redesign.)

A cross-partition query has no partition key in its filter, so the SDK must ask every physical partition and merge the results. It costs more RUs and more latency.

Example: SELECT * FROM c WHERE c.email = @e on a container partitioned by customerId checks all partitions, so the cost grows with the number of partitions. A query with WHERE c.customerId = @id goes to one partition. Pick a key that appears in your most frequent queries.

The id is a good partition key when most access is a point read by id and items are independent, such as a lookup of sessions or tokens.

Each item is then its own logical partition, which spreads the load perfectly and never reaches the 20 GB limit. The cost is that queries over many items are always cross-partition, and you cannot use transactional batches across items, because a batch must stay within one partition key.

Many-to-many in a document store is modelled by storing the ids on one or both sides, or with a separate link document.

Example: a student document holds courseIds: [3, 7], and you read the courses by id when needed. For a large or fast-changing relationship (a user following 1 million people), use link documents {userId, followsId} so that no document grows without limit. Keep a copy of the display name where you need to show lists fast.

An unbounded array makes the document grow forever: it slows every read and write, costs more RUs, and eventually hits the 2 MB item limit.

Example: embedding every comment of a popular post in the post document. After 50,000 comments each update rewrites a huge document. Embed only bounded, owned data (10-50 order lines) and put unbounded data in separate documents keyed by the parent id.

Update copies through the change feed or an event handler: when the source changes, an Azure Function reads the change and updates all documents that hold the copy.

Example: when a customer renames, a change feed processor finds the orders for that customer and updates the customerName field. The copies are eventually consistent, so copy only data that can be slightly stale, and keep the original in one place.

With session consistency, the client keeps a session token and sends it with its reads, which guarantees that it reads its own writes. Another instance does not have that token unless you pass it on.

To make a second API instance see the first's writes, return the session token to the caller (for example in a header) and have the caller send it on the next request, which the SDK accepts in RequestOptions.SessionToken. Otherwise the second instance may read slightly older data, though it is still in order.

CAP says that during a partition you choose consistency or availability. PACELC adds: Else (no partition) you choose between latency and consistency.

Cosmos DB's levels are a menu of those trade-offs: strong is consistent but with higher latency and no multi-region writes; eventual is fastest and cheapest but may be stale; the middle levels (bounded staleness, session, consistent prefix) sit between them. Session is the default and good for most apps.

Multi-region writes allow every region to accept writes, which lowers latency and improves availability, but the same item can be written in two regions at once, so conflicts are possible.

You choose a conflict resolution policy: last writer wins (the default, using a timestamp) or a custom merge procedure. Strong consistency is not available with multi-region writes. Design items to avoid simultaneous updates from different regions when you can.

code.title: Retry on throttling (429) with backoff

followUps:
The SDK retries automatically: by default up to 9 times, waiting for the time given in the x-ms-retry-after-ms header, within a total of 30 seconds, then throws a CosmosException with status 429.

You can change this through CosmosClientOptions.MaxRetryAttemptsOnRateLimitedRequests and MaxRetryWaitTimeOnRateLimitedRequests. Because the SDK retries quietly, your latency grows before you see any error, so monitor the count of 429s in metrics.

Create a new container with a better key and copy the data across, as the key cannot be changed in place.

Steps: pick a key from the query patterns and test the spread, create the container, copy with a container copy job or change feed, switch writers to both, verify counts, then move readers and delete the old container. If the problem is a few hot values, consider hierarchical partition keys or a synthetic key such as customerId-month.

Every indexed property adds RUs to every write, because each insert or update must also update the index. By default Cosmos DB indexes all paths.

On a write-heavy container, set the indexing policy to include only the paths you filter and sort on, and exclude the rest ("excludedPaths": [{"path": "/*"}] plus selected includes). Excluding large, unqueried properties can reduce write cost by a large fraction. Add composite indexes for queries that sort on multiple fields.

code.title: Out-of-order events: apply only newer versions

followUps:
Put a version number (or a row version) on each event, and in the read store apply an event only if its version is higher than the one stored.

Example: events 1, 3, 2 arrive. Apply 1, apply 3, skip 2 because 3 is stored. If a skipped event holds data that is not in later ones (a partial update), send the full state in each event instead of a delta. Per-key ordering (same partition key in Service Bus or Kafka) cuts the problem down further.

If Cosmos DB were the source of truth, the change feed would be the way to publish its changes to other systems, projections and caches, in order per partition key.

In this design SQL Server is the source, so the change feed is not the trigger, but it still helps for downstream work from the Cosmos read model (search index, notifications). It is a durable, ordered log of inserts and updates (deletes need soft-delete flags in the default mode).

Run a reconciliation job that samples or compares records in both stores and reports differences, and keep metrics for sync lag.

Example: nightly, take 10,000 random order ids, read them from SQL and Cosmos, compare version and key fields, and alert if more than 0.1% differ. Also track the age of the oldest unprocessed outbox row. A full rebuild of the read model from SQL should be possible and tested, as your recovery plan.

code.title: Cache-aside with a time-to-live

followUps:
In read-through, the cache itself loads missing data from the database; in write-through, every write goes to the cache, which writes it to the database at the same time. In cache-aside, your code does both jobs.

Read-through hides the loading logic in the cache layer (the app only asks the cache). Write-through keeps the cache always fresh, at the cost of slower writes. Redis does not do these on its own; HybridCache's factory delegate acts like read-through for your code.

Do not cache data that must be exact every time, such as account balances or stock at checkout, or that is user-specific and rarely repeated, or large and rarely reused objects.

Also never cache secrets or personal data carelessly, and avoid caching errors for long. Cache only where the hit rate is high and slight staleness is acceptable: product catalogue, configuration, lookup tables, expensive reports.

The app should keep working, just slower: treat the cache as optional, catch the exception, and read from the database.

Set short timeouts so a dead Redis does not make every request wait, and use a circuit breaker so you stop trying for a while. Watch the database: with a 95% hit rate the database suddenly receives 20 times more reads, so test that it can survive it, or shed load with rate limiting.

IMemoryCache has no size limit unless you set one, so it grows until the process runs out of memory, and the runtime does not know how big your entries are.

Set SizeLimit in MemoryCacheOptions and give each entry a Size (any unit you choose, such as 1 per item); entries beyond the limit are rejected or trigger compaction. Without it, caching per-user data can slowly take all the memory of the web app.

Local copies on other instances do not hear about the change, so they stay stale until their short expiry; the usual answer is a short L1 lifetime.

HybridCache keeps L1 lifetimes short (the LocalCacheExpiration option) and uses the distributed cache as the shared L2. For immediate invalidation across servers you need a notification channel, such as Redis pub/sub or a backplane, which HybridCache can use with some distributed cache setups (check the version you run).

Output caching stores the whole HTTP response for a route, and data caching stores objects that your code uses to build responses.

Output caching (app.UseOutputCache() and [OutputCache]) skips running the endpoint entirely, which is fastest but works only when the same response suits many users. It supports tags for invalidation: EvictByTagAsync("products"). Use data caching when the response differs per user but the data underneath is shared.

Deleting is safer because the next reader reloads the correct value from the database; updating the cache from the writer can leave a wrong value if two writers race.

Example: writer A reads price 10 and sets 12; writer B sets 15 in the database; their cache updates arrive in the other order, leaving 12 cached while the database holds 15. With delete, whoever misses next loads 15. A small window of staleness is still possible, which the TTL limits.

Absolute expiration removes the item a fixed time after it was created; sliding expiration extends the life each time the item is read.

Example: with absolute 10 minutes, a hot item is reloaded every 10 minutes, so it is never older than that. With sliding 10 minutes, a popular item may never expire and can be stale forever. So combine them: sliding for memory friendliness, plus an absolute maximum.

Use tags or keys that record the relationship: cache each page with a tag such as product:42, and when product 42 changes, evict everything with that tag.

Output cache and HybridCache support tags. Without tags, keep a set in Redis of page keys per product and delete them together, or put a version number for the product in the cache key so a change makes the old pages unreachable (they expire later).

code.title: Cache stampede prevented with single flight

followUps:
Keep a dictionary of in-flight loads per key, and let every caller await the same task, as in the example, or use a SemaphoreSlim per key.

var lazy = inFlight.GetOrAdd(key, k => new Lazy<Task<T>>(() => Load(k)));
try { return await lazy.Value; }
finally { inFlight.TryRemove(key, out _); }

Remove the entry when done so that failures are not cached forever. This works within one process; across servers you need a distributed lock or HybridCache, which does this for you.

A Redis lock can expire while the holder is still working, or the holder can crash, or a failover can lose the lock, so two processes may both think they own it.

Always set an expiry (TTL) so a crash cannot block everyone forever, use a unique token and release only if the token still matches, and never rely on the lock for correctness of money-like data. For cache loading it is acceptable, because the worst case is a few duplicate loads.

Pre-load the most important keys before sending traffic to the new instances, and spread the load over time with randomized TTLs.

Example: a startup job reads the top 1,000 products into the cache before the readiness probe passes, while running with limited concurrency such as 10 parallel reads. Also add jitter, for example TTL of 10 minutes plus a random 0-60 seconds, so keys do not all expire together. Deploy gradually, not all instances at once.

Synchronous replication waits for the replica to confirm the write before the commit returns, so no committed data is lost on failover but writes are slower. Asynchronous replication commits without waiting, which is faster but the replica can lag, and a failover may lose the last few transactions.

Availability groups in SQL Server allow both modes: synchronous commit between nearby nodes for high availability, asynchronous to a distant region for disaster recovery. Azure SQL does this for you.

Add ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly to the connection string; the connection is then routed to a readable replica (on the Premium, Business Critical or Hyperscale tiers).

Example: Server=...;Database=Orders;ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly;. Use a second DbContext with this connection string for reports and read-only queries. Because replication is asynchronous, the data can be slightly behind, so do not read-after-write from it.

High availability keeps the system running when a machine fails, using copies that are ready to take over; scaling adds capacity so it can handle more load.

A synchronous standby replica gives HA but does not make queries faster, because it only takes over on failure. A readable replica gives scale for reads and some HA. Do not confuse them: three copies of an overloaded database are still overloaded for writes.

code.title: Connection pool exhaustion

followUps:
The pool is keyed by the exact connection string (plus identity details), because connections with different settings are not interchangeable.
