Example: two strings that differ only in Application Name or by a trailing space make two separate pools, each of up to 100 connections, so your app can use double what you expected. Build the connection string from one configuration value and avoid putting per-user data in it.

Each function instance has its own pool, so 200 instances with a pool of 100 each could open 20,000 connections and exhaust the server.

Limit the pool size per instance (for example Max Pool Size=5), limit the scale-out of the function (WEBSITE_MAX_DYNAMIC_APPLICATION_SCALE_OUT), reuse static clients, and consider a connection gateway or proxy. Azure SQL has a connection limit by tier, so check it.

MARS (MultipleActiveResultSets=True) lets one connection have more than one open data reader or command at once; without it you get an error if you start a second query while a reader is open.

It interleaves the requests on one connection, so it is not parallel and it has some overhead. EF Core often needs it for lazy loading or when iterating one result while another query runs. Better is to load the first result completely (ToList) before the next query.

Partition elimination means the optimizer reads only the partitions that can hold the requested rows, ignoring the rest, when the query filters on the partitioning column.

Example: an Orders table partitioned by month. WHERE OrderDate >= '2026-03-01' AND OrderDate < '2026-04-01' reads only the March partition, while a query without a date filter reads all 36 partitions. Check the plan for Actual Partition Count. A function around the column can stop elimination.

A sliding window keeps a fixed period of data (for example 24 months) by adding a new partition at one end and switching the oldest out at the other, using metadata-only operations.

Each month: SPLIT RANGE to create the next empty partition, SWITCH PARTITION to move the oldest one to an archive table instantly (no row-by-row delete), then drop or archive it and MERGE RANGE to remove the empty boundary. It makes purging data very fast.

Azure SQL offers Hyperscale, which scales storage up to about 100 TB and adds named or HA replicas for reads, and elastic pools that share resources between many small databases.

Neither shards your data automatically. Elastic pools suit database-per-tenant designs where tenants peak at different times, so they share a budget. For true scale-out of writes you split data across databases yourself, with the elastic database client library or your own routing.

code.title: Consistent hashing: adding a shard moves little data

followUps:
Consistent hashing places both the shards and the keys on a ring, and each key belongs to the next shard clockwise, so adding a shard takes keys only from its neighbour instead of reshuffling everything.

With hash % N, going from 3 to 4 shards moves about 75% of the keys; with a ring only about 25% (1 divided by the new shard count). Virtual nodes (many points per shard) even out the load. The demo above shows the numbers.

Keep the shard map in a small, replicated database or config store, cache it in every app instance with a short TTL, and make it read-mostly.

The map is tiny (tenant id to shard), so caching is easy. Run it on a high-availability tier or in a multi-region store, and refresh the cache when a lookup hits a shard that says it no longer owns the tenant. Azure's Elastic Database tools have a shard map manager that does this.

Use a database per tenant when tenants need strong isolation, their own backups and restore, different sizes or compliance rules; use a shared database with a TenantId column when you have many small tenants and want low cost.

Database per tenant: easy to move or delete one tenant, but thousands of databases are hard to manage (use elastic pools). Shared: cheap and simple to operate, but a noisy tenant affects others and one bug can leak data, so use row-level security and a global query filter on TenantId. Many systems mix both: small tenants shared, big ones isolated.
